CHIEF COMPLAINT
Big toe pain and redness for two weeks, worsening over the past week.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a male who presents with pain and redness in his right big toe that has been occurring off and on for approximately two weeks, with significant worsening last week during a trade show convention where he was unable to walk the halls. He describes the pain as throbbing in nature with occasional sharp, stabbing quality, especially with movement or prolonged walking. He reports walking on his heel to minimize toe bending. Pain is exacerbated by light pressure, including contact with bed sheets at night. He denies a specific traumatic injury but became concerned when the toe became red and warm to the touch. He has tried ibuprofen 200mg twice daily without significant relief. Denies swelling at this time. Pain is worse with downward (plantar flexion) movement of the toe compared to upward movement.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies fever, chills, or systemic symptoms. Reports pain with range of motion of the big toe joint. Denies other joint involvement.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
None reported.

MEDICATIONS
Ibuprofen 200mg twice daily (over-the-counter, self-initiated).

ALLERGIES
Not documented.

FAMILY HISTORY
Not documented.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient enjoys cycling and reports riding over 800 miles on trails in the past year. Cycles with regular shoes on regular pedals. Frequently wears flip-flops. Also enjoys running and fishing. Works a job requiring him to be on his feet daily. Enjoys spicy Mexican food.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Inspection: Right big toe noted to be red. Palpation reveals tenderness over the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Bone spur palpated on top of the joint. Lateral aspect of the joint tender to palpation. Range of Motion: Limited dorsiflexion and plantarflexion with pain. Approximately 10 degrees of plantarflexion noted; pain increases with further plantarflexion to 20 degrees. Pain with medial and lateral deviation of the toe. Crepitus appreciated with passive motion, described as grinding sensation.

RESULTS
X-ray of right foot: Large bone spur on the top of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Significant loss of cartilage at the joint. Findings consistent with osteoarthritis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Hallux rigidus (first metatarsophalangeal joint osteoarthritis) with bone spur and cartilage loss.

Plan:
1. Orthotic insert for shoe to provide support and reduce motion at the affected joint.
2. Meloxicam once daily as anti-inflammatory medication. Counseled on potential side effect of gastric irritation; instructed to stop medication and call if experiences heartburn or substernal pain.
3. Continue regular work and daily activities to assess treatment effectiveness.
4. Follow-up appointment in two weeks to reassess symptoms and determine need for more invasive interventions, which may include intra-articular injection or surgical options (joint debridement or arthrodesis).
